title: DAT Patterns & the AIHA Workup: Warm Wears IgG, Cold Leaves C3d
summary: Read a monospecific DAT, tell warm AIHA from cold agglutinin disease and PCH, and work up a warm autoantibody safely with elution, IgG removal for phenotyping, and adsorption to unmask alloantibodies.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 40 Hit 9 (warm AIHA, CAD, PCH), Hit 19 (last-wash control), Hit 20 (IgG removal for phenotyping), Hit 21 (autoadsorption), Hit 23 (PCH) and Trap 2. Checked against Choi 2026, Nava Gutiérrez 2024, K H 2026, Kokoris 2022, Dara 2017, Katharia 2013 and Rodrigues 2024. Not taught: the reviewer’s “70–80% of AIHA” figure for warm AIHA (sources read say “most common” and CAD 15–25%), and CAD thermal amplitude 30–34 °C.

objectives: Interpret polyspecific and monospecific DAT results.
Distinguish warm AIHA, cold agglutinin disease and PCH by antibody, DAT pattern and tests.
Explain elution and the last-wash control.
Choose IgG-removal and adsorption methods to phenotype the patient and unmask alloantibodies.

scenes.title: Every cell on the panel reacts
scenes.altText: An antibody panel card with every cell positive (panagglutination), plus a DAT tube graded 3+. A patient card: hemolysis, needs blood. Question token: “Autoantibody — and is anything hiding underneath?”

cues.text: A patient with brisk hemolysis needs blood. The antibody screen is positive — and so is every cell on the panel.
The direct antiglobulin test is positive too. The patient’s own red cells are coated.
Is this an autoantibody? Which kind? And could a dangerous alloantibody be hiding underneath?

scenes.title: Normal: what the DAT asks
scenes.altText: A red cell drawn with nothing bound; antihuman globulin (AHG) added; no agglutination — DAT negative. Then a coated red cell: IgG molecules on the surface; AHG bridges coated cells into clumps — DAT positive. Next, the monospecific step: two reagent droppers labelled anti-IgG and anti-C3d test separately, producing a pattern (IgG ± C3d, or C3d only).

cues.text: The direct antiglobulin test asks one question: is something already stuck to the patient’s red cells in the body? Washed cells meet antihuman globulin. Nothing bound means no clumping.
If IgG or complement coats the cells, the antiglobulin reagent bridges them together and they clump: a positive DAT.
A positive polyspecific DAT is then repeated with monospecific reagents — anti-IgG and anti-C3d — to see what is on the cell.
That pattern names the likely mechanism. IgG, with or without C3d, points to a warm antibody. C3d alone points to a cold one.

scenes.title: What changes: warm AIHA, cold agglutinin disease, PCH
scenes.altText: Three columns. Warm AIHA: polyclonal IgG active at 37 °C; DAT IgG ± C3d; the most common AIHA; spleen removes coated cells (extravascular). Cold agglutinin disease: monoclonal IgM (mostly κ) that binds in the cold (optimal 0–4 °C); fixes complement; DAT C3d-positive, IgG-negative; cold agglutinin titer ≥ 1:64; 15–25% of AIHA. Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria: IgG anti-P that binds in the cold and lyses on rewarming (biphasic); Donath–Landsteiner test positive; < 1% of AIHA, half of cases under age 5.

cues.text: Warm AIHA is the most common type. Polyclonal IgG binds at body temperature, and the spleen removes the coated cells. DAT: IgG, with or without C3d.
Cold agglutinin disease: a monoclonal IgM binds best in the cold and switches on complement. DAT: C3d positive, IgG negative — with a cold agglutinin titer of at least 1 in 64.
Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria is rare — under one percent of AIHA, with half of cases in young children. An IgG antibody against P binds in the cold and destroys cells when they warm.
The Donath–Landsteiner test copies that: chill the patient’s blood, then warm it. Hemolysis only after cold-then-warm is a positive, biphasic result.

scenes.title: In the lab: unmasking what hides under a warm autoantibody
scenes.altText: Workflow cards. ① Elution: strip the antibody off the patient’s cells and test the eluate against panel cells; the last saline wash before elution is tested as a control — it must be negative, or leftover plasma antibody could be mistaken for eluted antibody. ② Phenotype the patient despite a positive DAT: remove bound IgG first (chloroquine diphosphate, EDTA–glycine acid or heat elution). ③ Adsorption: remove the autoantibody from plasma — autologous adsorption with the patient’s own (treated) cells if not transfused in the last 3 months; allogeneic adsorption with selected cells (e.g., R1R1, R2R2, rr) if recently transfused — then test the adsorbed plasma for alloantibodies. A note: one-third to one-half of AIHA patients have underlying alloantibodies.

cues.text: Step one: elution. Strip the antibody off the patient’s cells and test it against panel cells. First, test the last wash — it must be negative, or leftover plasma antibody could fool you.
Step two: phenotype the patient. Coated cells give false results, so remove the bound IgG first — with chloroquine diphosphate, an EDTA–glycine acid treatment, or heat.

Step three: adsorption. If the patient hasn’t been transfused in three months, adsorb the autoantibody onto their own treated cells. If they have, use selected donor cells instead — for example R1R1, R2R2 and rr cells.
Then test the adsorbed plasma. In AIHA, a third to a half of patients have alloantibodies hiding under the autoantibody — and those decide which blood is safe.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “DAT positive for C3d only — call it warm AIHA” is crossed out → “C3d only points to cold agglutinin disease or PCH.” Trap card: “Panreactive panel + positive DAT = just autoantibody; give any crossmatch-incompatible blood” is crossed out → “Adsorb first to exclude hidden alloantibodies.” Trap card: “Eluate reactive, so the antibody came off the cells” is crossed out → “Only if the last-wash control is negative.”

cues.text: Trap one: a C3d-only DAT isn’t warm AIHA. It points to cold agglutinin disease — or, in a young child, PCH.
Trap two: panagglutination isn’t “just autoantibody.” Adsorb the autoantibody first, so a hidden alloantibody isn’t missed.
Trap three: a reactive eluate means nothing if the last wash was positive. The control must be negative.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Monospecific DAT: IgG ± C3d = warm · C3d only = cold agglutinin disease or PCH”, “Elute (negative last wash) · remove IgG to phenotype · adsorb to unmask alloantibodies”.

cues.text: Let the monospecific DAT name the mechanism, then elute with a negative last wash, strip IgG to phenotype, and adsorb out the autoantibody to unmask alloantibodies.

props.label: DAT: IgG ± C3d = warm · C3d only = cold agglutinin disease or PCH
Elute (negative last wash) · strip IgG to phenotype · adsorb to unmask alloantibodies

explanation.what: Plain language: when a patient’s own red cells are coated, the lab works out what is on them and makes sure no other dangerous antibody is hiding. Scientific terms: DAT detects in-vivo IgG and/or complement (C3d) on red cells; monospecific reagents define the pattern. Warm AIHA = polyclonal IgG active at 37 °C (DAT IgG ± C3d); cold agglutinin disease = monoclonal IgM (mostly κ), complement-mediated (DAT C3d+, IgG−; titer ≥ 1:64); PCH = biphasic IgG anti-P (Donath–Landsteiner positive).
explanation.why: IgG-coated cells are cleared by Fc-receptor-bearing macrophages, mainly in the spleen. Cold IgM fixes complement and dissociates on warming, leaving C3d. In PCH, IgG binds in the cold and complement lyses cells on rewarming. Warm autoantibodies react with all panel cells and can mask alloantibodies.
explanation.measure: Elution with a negative last-wash control; IgG removal (chloroquine diphosphate, EDTA–glycine acid, heat) before phenotyping DAT-positive cells; adsorption — autologous if not transfused within 3 months, allogeneic (e.g., differential adsorption with R1R1, R2R2, rr cells) if recently transfused — then antibody identification on adsorbed plasma.
explanation.differs: Warm AIHA (IgG ± C3d) vs CAD (C3d only, IgM, cold agglutinin titer) vs PCH (C3d pattern; biphasic IgG anti-P; children). Autologous vs allogeneic adsorption.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: DAT pattern interpretation, Donath–Landsteiner test, last-wash control, phenotyping DAT-positive cells, and adsorption choice by transfusion history.

mnemonic.text: Warm wears IgG; cold leaves C3d behind — and PCH bites cold, kills warm.
mnemonic.explanation: IgG ± C3d marks warm AIHA; C3d only marks cold-reacting antibodies; PCH binds in the cold and lyses on warming.
mnemonic.limitation: Mixed AIHA shows both patterns; CAD can show weak IgG; drug-induced and DAT-negative AIHA exist; a positive DAT alone doesn’t prove hemolysis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with acrocyanosis in winter has hemolysis. Monospecific DAT: anti-IgG negative, anti-C3d 3+. Cold agglutinin titer is 1:512. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Correct. C3d-only DAT with a high cold agglutinin titer fits a complement-fixing cold IgM.
Incorrect. Warm AIHA is usually IgG-positive.
Incorrect. A DHTR typically shows IgG alloantibody on transfused cells.

options.text: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
options.rationale: Incorrect. That affects fetuses and newborns.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has sudden dark urine and anemia. DAT is C3d-positive, IgG-negative. Which test best confirms the suspected diagnosis?

options.rationale: Correct. PCH is confirmed by biphasic hemolysis — binding in the cold, lysis on warming.
Incorrect. A titer does not identify the biphasic IgG anti-P of PCH.
Incorrect. That screens for membrane disorders such as hereditary spherocytosis.

options.text: Acid elution with a positive last wash
options.rationale: Incorrect. A positive last wash invalidates an eluate and does not diagnose PCH.

questions.stem: A patient with warm AIHA and a panreactive antibody panel was transfused 3 weeks ago. Which approach best detects underlying alloantibodies?

options.text: Allogeneic (differential) adsorption with selected phenotyped cells, then test the adsorbed plasma
options.rationale: Correct. Recent transfusion means donor cells are present, so autologous adsorption could remove alloantibodies too.

options.text: Autologous adsorption with the patient’s own cells
options.rationale: Incorrect. Recently transfused donor cells in the sample could adsorb alloantibodies.

options.text: Issue any ABO-compatible unit, since all units are incompatible anyway
options.rationale: Incorrect. Hidden alloantibodies must be excluded first.

options.text: Repeat the panel with more cells
options.rationale: Incorrect. More cells still react with the autoantibody.

claims.text: Polyspecific DAT, then monospecific anti-IgG/anti-C3d to define warm vs cold pattern.
Warm AIHA: most common; polyclonal IgG at 37 °C; DAT IgG ± C3d; splenic Fc-receptor clearance.
CAD: monoclonal IgM-κ; complement; DAT C3d+, IgG−; titer ≥ 1:64; 15–25% of AIHA; optimal 0–4 °C.
PCH: biphasic IgG (P antigen) — binds cold, lyses on rewarming; Donath–Landsteiner positive; < 1% of AIHA; half under 5 years.
Last-wash supernatant is the negative control for elution; IgG removed by glycine/EDTA, heat or chloroquine diphosphate to phenotype DAT+ cells.
Autologous adsorption if not transfused within 3 months; allogeneic (differential R1R1/R2R2/rr) if transfused; 1/3–1/2 of AIHA patients have alloantibodies.
In CAD the IgM dissociates on warming, leaving C3d on the cells; PCH typically follows a viral infection in children.
claims.note: Consistent with the C3d-only pattern and pediatric predominance in consulted sources, but the dissociation step and post-viral timing were not stated explicitly.
